# The Speed-of-Light Tax

## The wall that does not move

Everything in the preceding chapters pushes toward consolidation, and within a
single region the case is close to unanswerable. Stretch the same store across
continents to keep a globally-synchronous source of truth, and you hit a wall
that no networking technology, present or future, moves: **the speed of
light.**

This chapter establishes that floor precisely, because the rest of the paper —
and any honest claim about what SD-WAN can do — depends on separating the part
of latency that is negotiable from the part that is not.

## Two latencies, added together

Wide-area round-trip time is the sum of two components with completely
different physics:

| Component | What it is | Can engineering reduce it? |
|---|---|---|
| **Propagation delay** | Time for the signal to physically travel the distance, at the speed of light in fiber | **No.** Fixed by distance on the chosen path. |
| **Everything else** | Queueing, congestion, jitter, packet loss → retransmits, and circuitous (non-geodesic) routing | **Yes — often dramatically.** This is the entire addressable surface. |

The first component is a tax levied by physics. The second is the gap between
the latency you *observe* and that physical floor — and on a congested or
badly-routed path that gap is frequently **2× to 10× the floor itself.** The
single most important framing in this paper is:

::: {.callout-important}
## Optimization attacks the gap, never the floor.
Every networking technique discussed in Chapter 4 — SD-WAN path selection,
forward error correction, jitter smoothing, clock distribution — operates on
the *"everything else"* component. None of them reduces propagation delay by a
single microsecond. The wins are real *because the gap is usually large*, but
the floor stays exactly where distance puts it.
:::

## The numbers

Light in optical fiber travels at roughly two-thirds of its vacuum speed —
about **200,000 km/s**, or **≈ 5 microseconds per kilometer**, or roughly
**1 millisecond per 200 km, one way.** That yields hard floors that no
optimization can beat:

| Path (approx. great-circle) | One-way propagation floor | Round-trip floor |
|---|---|---|
| Within a metro (~50 km) | ~0.25 ms | ~0.5 ms |
| Cross-region, same continent (~1,000 km) | ~5 ms | ~10 ms |
| New York ↔ London (~5,600 km) | ~28 ms | ~56 ms |
| New York ↔ Singapore (~15,300 km) | ~77 ms | ~153 ms |

These are *minimums assuming a perfectly straight fiber path.* Real paths are
longer — internet routes commonly run 1.5× to 3× the great-circle distance —
so observed propagation alone is typically well above these figures before any
congestion is added. Optimization can claw back the routing excess (Chapter 4);
it cannot go below the straight-line floor.

## Why strong consistency is a latency problem, not a bandwidth one

The crucial insight for database architecture is that **strong consistency
spends round trips, and round trips are priced in latency, not bandwidth.**

WAN bandwidth has grown enormously — moving terabytes between continents is
routine. But a strongly-consistent, synchronous commit does not need
bandwidth; it needs *agreement*, and agreement requires messages to travel to
other nodes and back:

- A synchronous commit that must be durable on a remote replica pays **at least
  one round trip** before it can acknowledge — every time.
- A consensus protocol (Paxos, Raft) committing through a quorum typically pays
  **one to two round trips** to the quorum members, and is gated by the
  *slowest* member it must hear from.

Across New York and London, that is a floor of ~56 ms *per synchronous commit*,
multiplied by every dependent operation in a transaction. No amount of fat pipe
changes it, because the limiting resource is the time for light to make the
trip, not the volume of data in flight.

## Tail latency: the part that actually hurts

There is a subtler reason distributed consistency suffers, and it sharpens what
Chapter 4 must target. Because a quorum commit waits for the *slowest* response
it needs, commit latency is governed by a **tail** statistic — the p99, not the
average. A path can have an excellent mean and still inflict terrible commit
latency if its tail is ugly, because every so often the one packet the quorum is
waiting on is the one that got queued, dropped, and retransmitted.

This matters because the "everything else" component — congestion, loss,
jitter — is precisely what *inflates the tail*, while propagation delay is
constant and therefore tail-neutral. So the addressable part of WAN latency is
also the part that disproportionately damages distributed databases. That is the
opening Chapter 4 exploits.

## What follows for architecture

Two conclusions fall directly out of the physics, and the rest of the paper
builds on them:

1. **Keep strong consistency inside a region.** At metro and intra-continental
   distances the propagation floor is sub-millisecond to a few milliseconds —
   synchronous consistency is effectively free there. This is why UIAO's
   single-region writer (Chapter 6) is not a limitation but a deliberate
   exploitation of the physics.
2. **Across regions, stop spending round trips.** The win is not a faster
   synchronous path — physics caps that — but an architecture that requires
   fewer synchronous crossings: asynchronous replication, bounded staleness,
   and merge-friendly data types (Chapter 5).

SD-WAN, the subject of the next chapter, lives entirely inside the gap between
observed latency and the floor. Understanding that it operates *there* — and
only there — is what lets us state precisely what it can and cannot do for
keeping large databases in sync.

## Summary

- WAN latency is propagation delay (fixed by distance, ~5 µs/km) plus
  everything else (congestion, loss, jitter, routing excess).
- Optimization addresses only the second component; the propagation floor is
  immovable. NY↔London is ~56 ms round-trip, minimum, forever.
- Strong consistency spends round trips, so it is a *latency* problem; fat
  bandwidth does not help it.
- Commit latency in a quorum is a *tail* statistic, and the tail is inflated by
  exactly the addressable (non-propagation) component — which is why network
  optimization can still help meaningfully.
- The architectural response: keep strong consistency intra-region; minimize
  synchronous crossings between regions.
